I prayed to see with my own eyes.
I look upon the ruined house.
A crash comes from within the halls.
To restrain the violence of murderous Zeus:
O Dionysus, Bacchus-throng. Or is it a form that you,
in the chambers where once
the body was hunted and captured:
Awe, O awe: or is it a stranger-dance.
And they, the mænads, who fled over the sea,
the spirits who excel in human prosperity,
entreat you with sea-play:
Io Bacchantes, Io Bacchantes.
Burn, burn the lone one.
Io, Io, saved, saved.
O Bromius, Bromius.
Chorus: Quickly, come into the houses,
reverence him, all who dwell within these halls.
See, column upon column, all
from the slaughter, the dark-flaming torch;
because Chorus: Fire has cast itself upon the earth,
or perhaps the thunder-struck ones
dwell, fallen with trembling bodies.
When the master turns everything upside down,
barbarian women, thus struck with fear,
whatever things inside the house were changed toward the gods,
appear to us, manifest, the Bacchic rites of Zeus.
Were they for us, or will the victory be gained again?
How, for the guard of murderous fate, did I
myself save him? Easily, I looked up.

...For the composite, which is changeable, is a follower of the simple and immutable, and it needs an intermediate bond for its connection to it. Nor should that which is able to be illuminated by the <unclear>Ideas</unclear> be participated in [directly], nor should the outpouring stop at these things, so that the last and [that which is] suspended from the principles [does not become disconnected]. It is necessary, therefore, to see the same <insert>beautiful A</insert> in two ways; and not only this, but also all the remaining <insert>all B</insert> forms: the Beautiful itself, the Equal, the Holy, and each of the beings. And to communicate them to all, to all that participate, and to see the secondary existences in lives [derived] from the truth. For neither does the worse coexist with the simple, nor with those that do not participate. For simplicity does not prevent the secondary existence, nor does the lack of participation. Therefore, it is necessary for the worse to coexist with lives that participate greatly—just as here with the just, the unjust; with the beautiful, the ugly; with the equal, the unequal. In this way, therefore, this life [exists]: the one itself and primarily, the other participating in its own way, [and] the one which is only sometimes participating. To this life, then, the insolent love is added as a secondary existence <note>original: "παρυφέστηκεν"</note> <gloss>a subordinate/subsidiary state</gloss>. Wherefore it is opposed to it; and opposite ends are set before it; and it uses clearer goals; and it is implanted in opposite lives. These things, then, about these matters. But that which has been collected here does not turn me, the young man, to an examination of the movements within him; but he shows himself not only as divinely erotic, but also as a prophet and wise man, having revealed his whole life, and having, as it were, dedicated the passions within him, just as those who sing songs before healings.

<summary>This page explains why subordinate or "worse" forms (like ugliness or injustice) necessarily exist alongside higher realities in the process of descent and participation, concluding with Socrates' role as a divinely inspired guide for the youth.</summary>

For even in the preceding [remarks] and in these things, which he used in his words, he appears rather as one not ignorant; and again [he says] more [in perplexity], "O Socrates, I have nothing to say"; and as one being naturally leader-like, [as one who] is borne toward heaven and from heaven [in his] intellect, and as one striving for power, height, and magnitude, he ascends to the middle, most high, and most powerful [realm] of the gods. Again, the appropriateness of Socrates' wonder is worthy of note; for after the refutation, he does not reproach him for his ignorance, but as one who does not know, as one who neither learned nor discovered, he asks, "How do you know and from where?" For this, at once, serves as a testimony of silence, and at the same time, as an appropriate healing, so that he may, in a certain way, refute [him] through himself. For just as the gods purify us and benefit us through themselves, and generally do not even act as self-movers, so too has Socrates engineered the manner of the refutation, where even the one being refuted refutes himself.

The one answering surely cleanses himself, and while delivering [himself] from ignorance, [he] brings the refutation upon himself; and [he] is the one cleansing and the one being cleansed; and the one refuting and the one being refuted. I do not know toward whom I have arrived at the refutation; nor toward the cleansing.

Cap. 41. What, then, does the "light of the soul" mean for Plato? It wishes to connect this to the light that is from it <note>the One</note>, but not to it <note>the One</note> itself. Why, then, is the light itself, that which is from it, not connected? Or is it connected according to the image of analogy, but no longer according to truth? For that <note>the One</note> does not endure the connection to another, which not even a point <note>geometric point</note> endures. But how is it "after" immediately? Is it because it appeared first among all things, or did it not perfectly emerge from the unapproachable? And generally, regarding what Plato said, later. Furthermore, the second thing after that, whatever it may be, as it is from that, proceeds along with all things in a manner that is everywhere indeterminate, without the opposition of determination. But as a second principle, it will set before us other concepts concerning itself and the things from it. For it is clear that we must assimilate our concepts to the things as much as possible. In the first, having become third, the three appear, proceed, and [continue] through all things that follow. I say "third," as if it appeared in the first intellect, and in everything in which the three exist. Nevertheless, the <term>mone</term> <gloss>remaining</gloss> prevails in the extreme, giving form to the others; in the last, the reversion; and in the middle, the procession. Wherefore, in every intellectual triad, the first is more stable, the second is more progressive, and the third is more reverting. Therefore, for these reasons, the twofold <term>mone</term> <gloss>remaining</gloss> was not hypothesized otherwise, since to remain is not to depart entirely from the generating cause, nor from its nature. And to revert is to circumscribe its own subsistence in the having-proceeded while remaining, so that it may be the same thing—having-proceeded and not-proceeded—not torn apart, but becoming something composed of both through the reverting property. For the third being such a whole, what other <term>mone</term> <gloss>remaining</gloss> could it have besides this reversion or this procession? Unless it is toward the things after these and produced from it. For the thing producing from itself in its own form and its own order the things after it would have the stable [nature] from the co-substantial <term>mone</term> <gloss>remaining</gloss>. Unless, perhaps, it should not be said that the producers remain, but that the things produced [remain] in the producers and in themselves. Or one must view the remaining of the producers according to the fact that they do not proceed together with the things produced.

What then? Does the whole such as this not revert to the first? Or will it make a reversion? Or if it first reverts to the generator, it must have proceeded, and it does not remain, as the puzzle [suggests]. There are types of structures: the *reticulate*, which all now use, [and] the ancient, which is called *incertum*. Of these, [in] beauty, the *reticulate* is such as to make cracks, because, being in all parts, it has dissolved beds and joints. *Incertum*, however, with one [stone] sitting above another and implicated in itself, [although it does] not look [as] smooth, yet provides a firmer structure than the *reticulate*. Both, however, are to be constructed with the utmost care, so that the walls, saturated with lime and sand, may last a long time. For soft and rare [stone], when constructed, draws out and sucks up the moisture from the mortar. But when there is a surplus and abundance of lime and sand [in] the wall, they have more moisture, they do not dry out quickly, but are held together by them. But when the wall has been constructed with a soft capacity, [and] the lime separates from the sand, they dissolve, the joints cannot cohere, and in time they make the walls ruinous. Therefore, one may notice this in some monuments which have been made around the city from marble or squared stones on the outside, [but] which, [with] the middle filled [with] structure, the mortar having withered with age, the structure perishes from rarity, [and] they dissolve from the ruin of the joints, [and] they dissipate into rubble. But if any wish to avoid this fault, having kept the middle hollow, a wall is to be set up on the inside with squared stone, or from terracotta, or from ordinary flints, [making] two-foot walls with these iron clamps and lead, [joined] together in the earth. Thus, not empty, but constructed in order, the work will be able to be [as] a living fortification. Because their beds and joints, sitting among themselves and bound in turn, do not allow the work to lean, nor do they allow the wall set up to slip [when] bound in itself. Therefore, the structure of those is not to be reproved. pages.translation: ...if a hot air makes the minds of men sharper: but it cools [them] and [makes them] slower. Since, however, the median nations are of the sharpest minds and the highest skill of [their] generations, they are for fortitude and magnanimity. I have said that the itinerary of the minds from the sun erupts from these. Those which refrigerate, are born in regions prepared for the vehemence of arms, in great, invincible [acts], without fear; but with slowness of mind, they rush without resistance. Without skill, they resist by their own counsels. Since, therefore, [mankind] is set among the things in the world and all nations are set in moderate mixtures: since, indeed, it possesses the space of the whole orb of the earth and the region in the middle of the world by the reason of things. Therefore, it stands most temperately toward both sides of the body and, indeed, in strengths, it is the most brave of nations. Just as the star of Mars in the heavens is very hot, and [Saturn] is very cold, the middle [planet] creates a temperate [state], by the same reason Italy, between the northern and the Indian [nations], by mixtures tempered from both sides, holds invincible [lands], and cools the itineraries of the barbarians by its counsel, and the thoughts of the Indians by a strong hand and by counsels. Thus, the divine mind placed the city of the Roman people in an excellent and temperate region, so that it might rule the orb of the earth. Since nature has created different regions by the inclinations of the sky for various generations, [and] since the nature of the spirits of the generations [is] distinct, the quality of the things which are born; I do not doubt that I should distribute the reasons of the buildings aptly to the nation and to the quality of the generations. I await from the skill of the things themselves to show [this]. Since I have set forth the reasons for the supreme power of the places, disposed by the nature of things; but how it is fitting to construct the reasons of the buildings to the inclinations of the sky for the generations, and [I] have described the nature of the figures in buildings, the limetars [and] the smaller separations, I will explain. No care should be greater for the architect than that the buildings should have the exactness of reason in proportions. Since, therefore, the reason of symmetry was set in the explanation of the arrangements: since, indeed, it [is] sharp: it is not shameful to add to the symmetry, either for use or for beauty, by additions, [and] by tempering. [If] it is said concerning symmetry that it is taken away or added, so that it is indicated that it was formed correctly; in appearance, nothing is missing. Another thing seems not to be in the appearance of the hand; another in a high place; not the same in an enclosure; [it is] different in the open, in which the works of great sapience are to be done at length. The sight does not seem to have the effect of sight; but it is often deceived in judgment by that which is placed, just as those things which are seen on the stage, the projection of columns, the figures of the signs of the spheres of the mechanics, [and] the projections, if they are placed without doubt to the plane rule. Similarly, in ships, the oars, if they are directed under the water, they are called broken; when they are directed, although they touch the surface of the water, they appear straight between them. When they are lowered under the water, by the transparency of the light, the image flowing from their bodies is sent back to the surface of the water; and these, by ignorance, are caused to be seen as a broken oar-blade. These, however, whether by the impulse of a simulacrum or by the outpourings of rays, as the physicists please, we see that the reason is such that the judgments of the eyes have a false aspect. Since, therefore, those things which are seen as false, but are not [false], but are presented to the eyes otherwise, it is necessary to make additions or subtractions according to the necessity or the place, so that nothing is missing from these works. This, however, is not explained by the ignorance of the masters; but when the length of the space of the place is built, the magnitude is [set] once. It follows that the proportioning to the beauty is made ready, so that [the things] will be clear to those sitting. Concerning which four reasons it is finished: in the first place, I will speak of the causes of the visual orb.
